books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1 (1835)

stimulus.text: “Amongst the novel objects that attracted my attention during my stay in the United States, nothing struck me more forcibly than the general equality of conditions. I readily discovered the prodigious influence which this primary fact exercises on the whole course of society, by giving a certain direction to public opinion, and a certain tenor to the laws. . . . The more I advanced in the study of American society, the more I perceived that the equality of conditions is the fundamental fact from which all others seem to be derived, and the central point at which all my observations constantly terminated.” — Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, Volume 1 (1835).
stimulus.source_note: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1 (1835), Introduction. Verbatim quotation (Reeve translation), verified against the Bill of Rights Institute excerpts. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Tocqueville's “general equality of conditions” refers most directly to which feature of American society?

options.misconception: Tocqueville saw great differences in wealth; his equality is about rank and opportunity, not equal money.

options.text: The right of every adult man and woman to vote in elections
options.misconception: Women, enslaved people, and many free Black men could not vote, so the vote was far from universal.

options.text: The absence of a fixed aristocracy, so rank followed effort, not birth
Equal legal rights for women and enslaved people
options.misconception: Tocqueville's America denied both groups political rights; his equality described white men.

rationales.A: Tocqueville's equality is about social rank, not equal wealth.
rationales.B: The vote was far from universal in the 1830s.
rationales.C: Tocqueville's “equality of conditions” means no hereditary aristocracy fixed a person's rank; birth mattered less than in Europe.
rationales.D: His equality described white men; women and enslaved people were excluded.
rationales.general:
1. Take his word “conditions,” not “wealth.” He means social rank, the standing a person is born into.
2. Compare with Europe. In France, birth set rank for life; in America, Tocqueville found rank fluid.
3. Keep the limit in view. This equality described white men in a society that still enslaved Black people and barred women from politics.
Background: Tocqueville visited in 1831 to study prisons and stayed to study the whole society, publishing the first volume in 1835.
Remember: equality of conditions is about rank, not riches.
